humans’ species-unique forms of cooperation—as well as their species-unique forms of cognition, communication,

Abstract
The ‘technological hypothesis’ proposes that gestural language evolved in early hominins to
enable the cultural transmission of stone tool-making skills, with speech appearing later in
response to the complex lithic industries of more recent hominins. However, no flintknapping
study has assessed the efficiency of speech alone (unassisted by gesture) as a tool-making
transmission aid. Here we show that subjects instructed by speech alone underperform in
stone tool-making experiments in comparison to subjects instructed through either gesture
